title: string_agg, array_agg, jsonb_agg
summary: Aggregates can build values: string_agg joins text, array_agg collects an array, jsonb_agg and jsonb_object_agg build JSON. Put ORDER BY inside the call, handle the NULLs a LEFT JOIN brings in, and aggregate each child list on its own to avoid join fan-out.

examples.title: string_agg and array_agg: element order, NULLs, DISTINCT, Turkish sorting

annotations.note: string_agg skips NULL inputs (Giriş has no owner); array_agg keeps them as NULL elements. ORDER BY inside the call orders the elements; the query's own ORDER BY only sorts the result rows. Without it the element order is unspecified.
DISTINCT removes duplicates before collecting, and FILTER drops the NULL that array_agg would otherwise keep. Can owns two tests and appears once.

The elements are compared in the column's collation. This database's default, C.UTF-8, compares code points, so Ç (U+00C7), İ (U+0130) and Ş (U+015E) sort after every ASCII letter and Giriş comes first. tr-x-icu gives the Turkish alphabet: C, Ç, ..., G, ..., I, İ, ..., S, Ş.
With no input rows array_agg returns NULL, not an empty array, and so do string_agg and jsonb_agg. coalesce supplies the empty value a client can iterate over.
SQLSTATE 42P10. Can has two ids, so "the distinct owners ordered by id" isn't defined. Order by the aggregated value, or remove duplicates in a subquery first.

examples.title: jsonb_agg and jsonb_build_object: a nested document per row, and the empty-list trap

annotations.note: REQ-EXPORT's padding row has t.id and t.title NULL, but the object built from them is not NULL: [{"id": null, "title": null}]. jsonb_agg_strict (PG 16) skips NULL inputs and wouldn't catch this either.
jsonb_build_object takes alternating keys and values. Each test row becomes one object, and jsonb_agg collects them in t.id order.
FILTER (WHERE t.id IS NOT NULL) drops the padding row, so the aggregate sees no input and returns NULL, and coalesce turns that into []. The same two steps apply to array_agg with '{}'.

The whole response document comes out of the database; the Go or TS layer can pass it through. jsonb doesn't preserve key order, so keys appear in jsonb's storage order, not the order of the call. Use the json variants if the text order matters.

jsonb_object_agg(key, value) builds an object; keys must not be NULL, and with jsonb a duplicate key keeps its last value. Aggregates can't be nested, so jsonb_object_agg(status, count(*)) is an error; count in a grouped subquery first.

examples.title: Two child lists: join fan-out, and one subquery per list

annotations.note: Each test row pairs with each tag row of the same requirement, and the aggregates see all 6 pairs: count says 6, every tag appears twice. REQ-EXPORT gets {NULL} from its padding row. count(DISTINCT t.id) and array_agg(DISTINCT g.tag) would hide the damage but still build the product, and array_agg(DISTINCT t.title) would also merge two different tests that happen to share a title.

ARRAY(subquery) is a correlated subquery per requirement, so each list is built from its own table with its own ORDER BY, and nothing multiplies. It returns {} when the subquery finds no rows. For JSON, the same shape is (SELECT coalesce(jsonb_agg(...), '[]') FROM ... WHERE ... = r.id), or a LATERAL subquery per child.

use_cases: API list endpoints that return parent rows with nested children as JSON, in one query instead of 1 + N
Exports and reports with a readable cell such as 'Can, Zeynep' (string_agg) or a tag list (array_agg)
Lookup maps sent to a frontend: jsonb_object_agg(code, label) gives {"REQ-1": "Login", ...}
Collecting ids to pass on in one parameter: array_agg(id) feeding = ANY($1) in a later query
strengths: One query returns the response shape, so the ORM-style 1 + N queries (one per parent for its children) disappear
ORDER BY inside the aggregate gives deterministic lists with the collation you choose, including Turkish order
jsonb_build_object and jsonb_agg produce valid JSON with correct escaping; there is no string concatenation to get wrong
string_agg skips NULLs, unlike JS's join (empty string) or Java's String.join (the text "null")
weaknesses: NULL behaviour differs per function: string_agg skips NULLs, array_agg and jsonb_agg keep them, and all return NULL for no rows
Over a LEFT JOIN, the padding row ends up in the list ({NULL}, or an object of nulls) unless you FILTER it out
Every collected value is built in memory and a single value is capped at 1 GB, so whole-table exports belong in COPY or a streamed cursor, not one jsonb_agg
JSON built in SQL is untyped to the application; Go or TS still needs a schema check (struct tags, zod) on the way in

pitfalls.title: ORDER BY in the wrong place
pitfalls.detail: The query's ORDER BY sorts result rows, not the elements of an aggregate. Inside the call it goes after all arguments: string_agg(title ORDER BY title, ', ') parses as a one-argument string_agg and fails with function string_agg(text) does not exist.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT string_agg(title ORDER BY title, ', ') FROM test_cases
pitfalls.good: SELECT string_agg(title, ', ' ORDER BY title) FROM test_cases

pitfalls.title: jsonb_agg over a LEFT JOIN
pitfalls.detail: A parent without children yields [{"id": null, ...}], or [null] when you aggregate a bare column. Filter the padding row out and coalesce the empty case.
pitfalls.good: coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id)) FILTER (WHERE t.id IS NOT NULL), '[]')

pitfalls.title: Two child lists from two joins
pitfalls.detail: Joining tests and tags to the same requirement multiplies them, and every list and count is inflated. DISTINCT hides it at a cost. Aggregate each child in its own subquery.
pitfalls.bad: FROM requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON ... LEFT JOIN tags g ON ... GROUP BY r.id
pitfalls.good: SELECT r.code, ARRAY(SELECT ... FROM test_cases t WHERE t.requirement_id = r.id ORDER BY ...), ARRAY(SELECT ... FROM tags g WHERE g.requirement_id = r.id ORDER BY ...) FROM requirements r

pitfalls.title: Code-point order for Turkish names
pitfalls.detail: Under C.UTF-8, Çağla, İrem and Şule sort after Zeynep. Name the collation in the aggregate's ORDER BY, or declare the column with it.

quiz.q: owner holds 'Zeynep', NULL and 'Can' (in id order). What does `string_agg(owner, ', ' ORDER BY id)` return?
quiz.why: string_agg concatenates the non-NULL inputs only; the NULL contributes neither a value nor a delimiter.

quiz.q: REQ-EXPORT has no tests. What does `jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id))` give for it after `requirements r LEFT JOIN test_cases t ... GROUP BY r.id`?
quiz.why: The LEFT JOIN supplies one padding row, and jsonb_build_object turns its NULLs into an object, which jsonb_agg collects.

quiz.q: A requirement has 2 tests and 3 tags. Joined to both tables and grouped by requirement, what does count(t.id) return?
quiz.why: Each test row pairs with each tag row of the same requirement, so the group holds 2 x 3 rows, all with a non-NULL t.id.

quiz.q: Which call returns the titles in alphabetical order?
options: string_agg(title, ', ') with ORDER BY title at the end of the query
quiz.why: Element order is set inside the call, after all arguments. The query-level ORDER BY sorts rows, and the third form is a call to a one-argument string_agg that doesn't exist.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Aggregate Expressions (ORDER BY inside the call)
PostgreSQL docs: JSON Types (json vs jsonb, key order, duplicate keys)

body:
## Concept

Not every aggregate reduces a group to a number. Some collect it:

- `string_agg(value, delimiter)` joins text,
- `array_agg(value)` builds an array,
- `jsonb_agg(value)` builds a JSON array, and `jsonb_object_agg(key, value)` a JSON object.

They follow the same rules as `count`: one result per group, computed after `WHERE`. What
is new is that their result depends on the **order** of the input, and that order is
unspecified unless you write `ORDER BY` inside the call.

Together with `jsonb_build_object`, they turn a parent-child relationship into a nested
document in one query: one row per requirement, its tests as a JSON array. That is the
shape an API returns, and it replaces the "one query for the parents, one per parent for
the children" pattern ORMs fall into.

Two things go wrong regularly. NULLs: `string_agg` skips them, `array_agg` and
`jsonb_agg` keep them, and a LEFT JOIN supplies one for every parent without children.
Fan-out: joining two child tables to the same parent multiplies their rows before any
aggregate sees them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** `', '.join(sorted(names))` is `string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)`,
  except that `join` raises `TypeError` on `None` where `string_agg` skips it. `sorted()`
  on `str` compares code points, like C.UTF-8 here; Turkish order needs a collation
  library, as it needs `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` here.
- **JS:** `[a, null, b].join(', ')` turns the null into an empty string (`"a, , b"`);
  `Intl.Collator('tr')` is the browser's Turkish collation.
- **Java:** `Collectors.joining(", ")` appends the text `null` for null elements;
  `Collator.getInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"))` sorts Turkish.
- **Go:** `strings.Join(slices.Sorted(...), ", ")`, and `golang.org/x/text/collate` for
  Turkish order. A `jsonb_agg` result scans into `json.RawMessage` and can go straight
  into the HTTP response.
- **ORMs:** eager-loading two collections through joins hits the same fan-out as
  example 3, which is why ORMs usually load each collection with a query of its own.

## Design notes

Build JSON in SQL when the response is a projection of the query: list endpoints,
exports, dashboards. The application passes the bytes through and stays thin. Build
objects in Go or TS when the data feeds domain logic that wants typed values. Either way,
make empty lists `[]`, never `null`: `coalesce(... FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL),
'[]')`.

Give each child list its own subquery (`ARRAY(...)`, a scalar `(SELECT jsonb_agg(...)
...)`, or `LATERAL`). One `GROUP BY` over two child joins is wrong by construction, and
`DISTINCT` inside the aggregates only hides it.

Prefer `jsonb_agg` and `jsonb_build_object` unless you need the exact text (key order,
duplicate keys) that the `json` variants keep. For Turkish text, put the collation where
the ordering happens (`ORDER BY name COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` inside the aggregate) or on the
column, if Turkish order is what the column means everywhere.

files.examples/01_lists.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.aggregation.agg-funcs): an aggregate can build a value, not just a number.
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id    int PRIMARY KEY,
  suite text NOT NULL,
  title text NOT NULL,
  owner text              -- NULL: nobody owns it yet
);
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (1, 'auth',   'Şifre sıfırlama',      'Zeynep'),
  (2, 'auth',   'Çıkış',                'Can'),
  (3, 'auth',   'Giriş',                NULL),
  (4, 'auth',   'İki adımlı doğrulama', 'Can'),
  (5, 'export', 'CSV dışa aktarım',     'Ilgaz');

-- The order of elements goes inside the call. string_agg skips NULLs;
-- array_agg keeps them.
SELECT suite,
       string_agg(owner, ', ' ORDER BY id) AS owners_text,
       array_agg(owner ORDER BY id)        AS owners_array,
       array_agg(DISTINCT owner ORDER BY owner) FILTER (WHERE owner IS NOT NULL)
         AS distinct_owners
FROM test_cases
GROUP BY suite
ORDER BY suite;

-- ORDER BY title compares in the column's collation: C.UTF-8 sorts by code
-- point, so Ç, İ and Ş come after Z. Name the Turkish collation to fix it.
SELECT string_agg(title, ', ' ORDER BY title)                     AS by_code_point,
       string_agg(title, ', ' ORDER BY title COLLATE "tr-x-icu") AS turkish
FROM test_cases
WHERE suite = 'auth';

-- No input rows: array_agg gives NULL, not an empty array.
SELECT array_agg(title ORDER BY title)                 AS raw,
       coalesce(array_agg(title ORDER BY title), '{}') AS or_empty
FROM test_cases
WHERE suite = 'billing';

-- With DISTINCT, the ORDER BY may only use the aggregated expression.
SELECT array_agg(DISTINCT owner ORDER BY id) FROM test_cases;
files.examples/02_json.sql:
CREATE TABLE requirements (id int PRIMARY KEY, code text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id             int PRIMARY KEY,
  requirement_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  title          text NOT NULL,
  status         text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES (1, 'REQ-LOGIN'), (2, 'REQ-EXPORT');
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (10, 1, 'Valid password', 'passed'), (11, 1, 'Locked account', 'failed');

-- One JSON document per requirement, tests nested. REQ-EXPORT has no tests:
-- the LEFT JOIN gives it one all-NULL row, and that row becomes an object.
SELECT r.code,
       jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id, 'title', t.title) ORDER BY t.id)
         AS tests
FROM requirements r
LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id
GROUP BY r.id
ORDER BY r.code;

-- Fixed: FILTER drops the padding row, coalesce turns "no rows" into [].
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'code', r.code,
         'tests', coalesce(
           jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('id', t.id, 'title', t.title)
                     ORDER BY t.id) FILTER (WHERE t.id IS NOT NULL),
           '[]'::jsonb)
       ) AS doc
FROM requirements r
LEFT JOIN test_cases t ON t.requirement_id = r.id
GROUP BY r.id
ORDER BY r.code;

-- A JSON object instead of an array: key/value pairs from a grouped subquery.
SELECT jsonb_object_agg(status, n) AS tests_by_status
FROM (SELECT status, count(*) AS n FROM test_cases GROUP BY status) AS s;
